questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The Gini coefficient from a table of incomes
questions.learningObjective: compute the Gini coefficient from a small income distribution
questions.stem: Incomes for five households ranked from poorest to richest are 10, 20, 30, 40 and 100. What is the Gini coefficient of this distribution?

options.text: 0.20, which is the weighted sum of incomes divided by twice the number of households times the mean
options.misconception: drops the factor of two from the pairwise formula, so the result is half the true value

options.text: 0.40, which is one less than twice the area of 0.30 under the Lorenz curve
0.30, which is the area under the Lorenz curve, reported instead of the gap below the line of equality
options.misconception: reports the area under the curve rather than the area between the curve and the line of equality

options.text: 0.60, which is one less the coefficient, obtained by subtracting rather than doubling the area
options.misconception: subtracts the area instead of subtracting it from one after doubling it

questions.explanation: The mean income is 200 over 5, that is 40, and the Lorenz curve passes through the points 0, 0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.50 and 1, so the area under it, summing five trapezoids of width 0.2, is 0.005 plus 0.02 plus 0.045 plus 0.08 plus 0.15, that is 0.30. The coefficient is one less twice that area, so 1 less 0.6, which is 0.40. The second route is the rank formula, the weighted sum 2i less n less 1 times income, which is minus 40 minus 40 plus 80 plus 400, that is 400, over the 25 households squared times the mean of 40, which is 1,000, again 0.40. Omitting the factor of two in the second route halves the answer, which is the most common way the number is got wrong.
questions.hint: Build the Lorenz curve from the cumulative income shares and take the area under it, then check with the rank formula.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The Gini as an area between two curves
questions.learningObjective: state the geometric definition of the Gini coefficient
questions.stem: The Gini coefficient is defined as an area. Which area is it?

options.text: The area between the Lorenz curve and the horizontal axis, which is the share of income below the median
options.misconception: names the area under the curve, which is large even when the distribution is perfectly equal

options.text: The area between the Lorenz curve and the vertical axis, which measures the share of people above the median
options.misconception: names the complementary area, which is near one for equality rather than near zero

options.text: The area between the Lorenz curve and the line of perfect equality, divided by the area under the line of equality
The area of the rectangle under the highest income and the lowest income, with no reference to equality
options.misconception: refers to a range rather than to a comparison with the distribution of an equal society

questions.explanation: The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of people, and the line of equality is the diagonal, since a distribution in which everyone has the same income gives a straight line at 45 degrees. The Gini is the area between the two curves divided by the area under the diagonal, so a distribution in which everyone has the same income gives an area of zero and the whole triangle, giving a coefficient of zero, while a distribution in which one person has everything gives the whole triangle as the gap and a coefficient of one. The normalising division by the area under the line of equality is what makes the coefficient comparable across countries, which a raw area would not be.
questions.hint: Ask which curve represents an equal distribution, and what the gap between them measures.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why the Gini is insensitive to a transfer at the bottom
questions.learningObjective: show that the Gini responds less to redistribution at the bottom of the distribution
questions.stem: Five households ranked from poorest to richest have incomes of 10, 20, 30, 40 and 100, giving a Gini coefficient of 0.40. Two transfers of 5 are then made from the richest household. If the first is made to the poorest and the second to the household with 30, what are the two new Gini coefficients?

options.text: 0.36 and 0.38, so moving income to the bottom cuts the coefficient twice as much as moving it to the middle
0.38 and 0.36, so a transfer to the middle of the distribution moves the coefficient more than one to the bottom
options.misconception: reverses the two answers, which contradicts the weights in the rank formula

options.text: 0.35 and 0.35, so a transfer of the same size always changes the coefficient by the same amount
options.misconception: assumes the coefficient depends only on the size of the transfer and not on where it is made

options.text: 0.40 and 0.40, so a transfer between households within one distribution cannot change its inequality
options.misconception: assumes inequality is invariant to a redistribution, which is what the index exists to measure

questions.explanation: After the first transfer the incomes are 15, 20, 30, 40 and 95, still totalling 200 with a mean of 40, and the rank formula gives minus 60 minus 40 plus 80 plus 380, that is 360, over 1,000, so 0.36. After the second they are 10, 20, 35, 40 and 95, and the weighted sum is minus 40 minus 40 plus 80 plus 380, that is 380, over 1,000, so 0.38. The first transfer removes 5 from a household 8 times the mean and adds it to one a quarter of the mean, while the second adds it to a household three quarters of the mean, so the gap from the mean widens less. The ratio of the incomes the weights attach to is the whole explanation, and it is the standard objection to using the Gini to evaluate transfers that go to the poorest.
questions.hint: Recompute the weighted sum of incomes for each new distribution and divide by households squared times the mean.

questions.topic: The Lorenz curve
questions.learningObjective: interpret a point on a Lorenz curve
questions.stem: A Lorenz curve for a country passes through the point 0.40 of the population holding 0.10 of total income. What does that point tell you?

The richest 40 percent of the population receive a tenth of the country's income
options.misconception: reads the population axis from the top rather than from the left, which reverses the point

options.text: The median household receives 40 percent of the country's income
options.misconception: confuses a point on the curve with the height of the curve at the midpoint of the population

options.text: Ten percent of households have no income at all
options.misconception: treats a low cumulative share at 40 percent of people as proof of zero income for some of them

A point at 0.40 and 0.10 therefore says the bottom 40 percent share 10 percent of income, which is a quarter of what an equal distribution would give them, and that ratio is a compact way to state how far the bottom of the distribution falls short. The curve is built by plotting one point per equal-sized group, so the point directly above 0.5 on the horizontal axis, not 0.40, is the one that speaks to the median.

questions.topic: Mean and median of a skewed distribution
questions.learningObjective: compute the mean and the median of a skewed income distribution
questions.stem: Four households have annual incomes of 10, 20, 30 and 140. What are the mean and the median, and what does the gap between them indicate?

options.text: A mean of 25 and a median of 50, reversing the two, because the mean is always below the median
options.misconception: reverses the two measures, which is the opposite of the usual pattern for a right skewed distribution

options.text: A mean of 50 and a median of 25, so the mean is twice the median because one household's income is extreme
A mean of 50 and a median of 30, using the 30 as the middle value after discarding the 140
options.misconception: discards the largest observation instead of letting it influence the mean, which is the whole difference

options.text: A mean and a median both of 50, on the argument that four households must divide the total evenly
options.misconception: assumes an even split among four households, which the listed incomes contradict

questions.explanation: The total is 200 over 4 households, so the mean is 50, while the median is the average of the two middle values, 20 and 30, which is 25. The second route is the same computation written as a total divided by a count, and the check is that the mean exceeds the median because the distribution is right skewed, since one household at 140 pulls the mean up by 25 while leaving the middle two values untouched. That gap is why a policy described in terms of the average income of all households can leave the household at the middle of the distribution worse off, and it is the reason the two measures have to be named before any statement about typical living standards is accepted.
questions.hint: Divide the total income by the number of households, then average the two middle values.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The Theil index
questions.learningObjective: compute a Theil index from a small income distribution
questions.stem: A distribution of five households ranked from poorest to richest has incomes of 10, 20, 30, 40 and 100, and its mean is 40. What is the Theil index, computed as the average of each household's share of the mean multiplied by the logarithm of that share? Report the number to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The five income shares of the mean are 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 and 2.5, and the summands are 0.25 times the natural log of 0.25, which is minus 0.3466, 0.5 times minus 0.6931, which is minus 0.3466, 0.75 times minus 0.2877, which is minus 0.2158, 1 times zero, and 2.5 times 0.9163, which is 2.2907. The sum is 1.3817 and dividing by 5 gives 0.2763, which is the Theil T. The second route is the generalised entropy form, minus half the average of the log deviation from the mean, which for the five log deviations that sum to minus 1.4508 gives 0.1451, so the two indices are not interchangeable and the definition has to be stated. What the Theil buys over the Gini is decomposability, which is the subject of the next item.
questions.hint: Divide each income by the mean, multiply each ratio by its own logarithm, and average the five results.

questions.topic: Decomposing the Theil across two groups
questions.learningObjective: decompose an inequality index into within-group and between-group parts
questions.stem: Four households have incomes of 10, 30, 60 and 100, so the mean is 50. The first two form region A with a mean of 20 and the last two form region B with a mean of 80. Using the Theil index, what is the part of measured inequality that comes from the difference between the two regional means?

options.text: 0.051, being what is left after the between-region part, so the regions are nearly equal in income
options.misconception: reports the within-region residual, which is small here precisely because the regions differ so much

options.text: 0.193, being 0.2 times the log of 0.4 plus 0.8 times the log of 1.6, and the rest is within region
0.244, which is the whole Theil index, on the argument that all of it is attributable to regional differences
options.misconception: counts all of the measured inequality as between-region when part of it is inside the regions

options.text: 0.600, which is the ratio of the two regional means, 80 over 20, taken as an inequality index
options.misconception: uses a ratio of means as if it were a Theil component, which measures something else entirely

questions.explanation: Each region holds half the households, so the between-region term is 0.5 times 0.4 times the log of 0.4, which is 0.2 times minus 0.9163, or minus 0.1833, plus 0.5 times 1.6 times the log of 1.6, which is 0.8 times 0.4700, or 0.3760, and the sum is 0.1927. The whole index is 0.2442, computed from the four income shares of 0.2, 0.6, 1.2 and 2, so the within-region part is the difference, 0.0514, and the two add back to the total exactly, which is the decomposability property that the Theil has and the Gini does not. The practical use is that a rise in the total can be attributed to a widening of regional differences or to more inequality inside regions, and the two call for different policies.
questions.hint: Weight each regional mean's log deviation by its population share, then subtract the result from the whole index.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The Palma ratio
questions.learningObjective: compute the Palma ratio and relate it to the Gini
questions.stem: Annual incomes of 10, 20, 30, 40 and 100 are recorded for five households ranked from poorest to richest. What is the Palma ratio, that is the share of income going to the richest fifth divided by the share going to the poorest two fifths? Report the number to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The richest fifth of five households is the single household at 100, and the poorest two fifths are the two households at 10 and 20, so the ratio is 100 over 30, which is 3.33. The second route uses the income shares of the total of 200: 50 percent for the top fifth against 15 percent for the bottom two fifths, and 50 over 15 is again 3.33, since the total cancels. The measure is built on the empirical regularity that the income share of the middle 60 percent is fairly stable across countries, so the top-to-bottom ratio carries most of the movement; what it discards is exactly the detail at the bottom that the Gini is criticised for under-weighting.
questions.hint: Add the incomes of the poorest two fifths and divide the top fifth's income by that sum.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Income shares and the identity that they sum to one
questions.learningObjective: state why income shares sum to one and what breaks the identity
questions.stem: A distribution gives the shares of income accruing to labour, capital, land and rent as 0.55, 0.25, 0.10 and 0.10. What does the requirement that the shares sum to one let an analyst do, and what would break it?

options.text: It lets each share be attributed to a household type, and it breaks if two types receive income jointly
options.misconception: misreads the identity as a statement about households rather than about sources of income

options.text: It fixes the size of the transfer needed to equalise the shares, and it breaks if taxes are not lump sum
options.misconception: supposes the identity is a policy constraint, when it is only an accounting statement

options.text: It implies the shares are equal when the distribution is efficient, and it breaks if any distortion exists
options.misconception: reads an accounting identity as a statement about the efficiency of the economy

options.text: It lets any one share be computed from the others, and it breaks if retained earnings or imputed rents are omitted from one of them

questions.explanation: Every unit of income is received by someone, so the shares by source must exhaust the total, and that is what lets an analyst infer one from the others, which is how a labour share is obtained as one less capital, land and rent. The identity breaks in practice for reasons of measurement rather than of accounting: corporate saving is retained inside a firm and appears as a company's profit rather than as someone's dividend, and owner-occupied housing is treated as though the owner paid themselves rent. Neither omission changes the total, but each changes which share a residual ends up in, and the labour share is usually the residual of last resort.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be counted for the shares to exhaust total income.

questions.topic: The labour share of national income
questions.learningObjective: compute the labour share from the income side of the accounts
questions.stem: Gross domestic product at market prices is 1,000. Compensation of employees is 620, net taxes on production and imports are 80, and the operating surplus is 300. What is the labour share of gross domestic product? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The labour share is compensation of employees over gross domestic product at market prices, so 620 over 1,000, that is 0.62. The check is that the income side has to close, and 620 of compensation plus 300 of operating surplus plus 80 of net taxes is 1,000, so the three components account for the whole of output and the share is internally consistent. The alternative denominator is worth naming: compensation over value added at basic prices, which is 620 over 920, gives 0.674, a higher figure, and the two are both quoted in the literature because they answer different questions, one about wages as a share of all output and one about wages as a share of the value added in production.
questions.hint: Divide compensation of employees by gross domestic product at market prices, and check that the income side adds up.

questions.topic: Gross labour compensation and the labour share
questions.learningObjective: distinguish wages from total labour compensation in measuring the labour share
questions.stem: Gross domestic product at market prices is 1,000. Wages and salaries paid to employees are 560 and employers' social contributions are 60, so compensation of employees is 620. What is the labour share measured on wages alone, and what is it on total compensation?

options.text: 0.62 measured on wages alone and 0.68 on total compensation, reversing which numerator is the larger
options.misconception: takes wages alone to be the larger figure, which contradicts the stated contributions

options.text: 0.56 and 0.62, but the two must always be reported together since neither is the true labour share
options.misconception: accepts both figures but denies that either is a usable definition of the share

options.text: 0.56 measured on wages alone and 0.62 on total compensation, so the choice of definition moves the share by 6 points
0.06 and 0.62, reporting the contributions themselves as the share of wages paid by employers
options.misconception: reports the contribution as a share rather than adding it to the wage to form compensation

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why estimates of the labour share differ
questions.learningObjective: explain why measured labour shares differ across studies
questions.stem: Estimates of the labour share of income differ across countries and across studies even when the underlying data are careful. What are the main reasons, and why is it hard to settle the question?

answer.exemplar: The labour share is a ratio whose numerator is measured directly and whose denominator is also a total, so it is not a difference between two independently estimated quantities, but its components are measured very unevenly. Wages come from employer surveys, tax records and household surveys that disagree on who is employed and for how long, and self-employment income has to be split into a return to labour and a return to capital using an assumption that no data can verify. Profits are a residual, so any error in the estimate of output or of non-labour income lands in the capital share, which is why a sector that grows fast, such as one with many small firms, can show a rising profit share with no change in bargaining power at all. The reason the question resists settling is that the two candidate explanations, a change in bargaining power and a change in the composition of output towards capital-intensive sectors, predict the same movement in the aggregate share, and only evidence that separates them can tell the two apart.

questions.explanation: The aggregate share is a weighted average of the sectoral shares, with the weights being labour's share of employment, so a composition shift towards sectors with low labour shares lowers the aggregate with no change in any firm's conduct. That is the first alternative explanation and it is a real one; the second is a change in the distribution of bargaining power within sectors. Both are consistent with a falling share, and the empirical work that tries to separate them has to compare within-sector shares with between-sector shifts, which is possible only where the data are detailed enough. The measurement problems compound the problem, because a residual capital share absorbs errors in output, and a fall in a measured labour share is therefore a statement about a ratio of two imperfect numbers.
questions.hint: Ask whether the aggregate share is a weighted average of sectoral shares, and what changes the weights.

questions.topic: Rent and the difference between income and profit
questions.learningObjective: separate economic rent from a return to a factor at its opportunity cost
questions.stem: A firm's revenue is 400 and its variable costs are 250. It uses a fixed amount of capital worth 100, and the return on capital required to cover that cost is 10 percent. What is the economic rent the firm earns? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The quasi-rent is revenue less variable cost, 400 minus 250, that is 150, and the opportunity cost of the fixed capital is 100 times 0.10, that is 10, so the economic rent is the 150 minus 10, which is 140. The second route is the same calculation as profit net of the normal return, where profit is 150 before any charge for capital and the normal charge is 10. The distinction is what makes rent a distributional object rather than a productivity object: the 10 is what the same capital would earn elsewhere and is paid for by the consumer's price, whereas the 140 is a surplus available to be shared, and a tax aimed at rent has to be aimed at income that would otherwise accrue to the owner regardless of how efficiently the asset is used.
questions.hint: Take revenue less variable cost, then subtract the return the fixed capital could have earned elsewhere.

options.misconception: confuses a share of the total with a ratio of averages, which differ whenever the group sizes differ

options.text: The share of the population with income above the mean, since the top tenth must be above the mean
options.misconception: confuses a percentile of the distribution with the mean, which is a different order statistic

questions.topic: An absolute poverty line
questions.learningObjective: define an absolute poverty line and state what changes it over time
questions.stem: An absolute poverty line is set at a level fixed in real terms. What follows from fixing it that way?

options.text: A real fall in income can move households into poverty even though the line has not changed at all
Poverty measured against it is constant, since the line is fixed and the households are counted as they are
options.misconception: treats a fixed line as a fixed count, ignoring that incomes move while the line does not

options.text: The line must be raised every year to remain constant in real terms, which makes it an index
options.misconception: confuses an absolute line with an indexed one, which is the opposite convention

options.text: It measures inequality within the population, since a fixed line divides households into two groups
options.misconception: confuses a poverty count with a measure of the shape of the whole distribution

questions.explanation: An absolute line answers whether a household can buy a fixed basket of necessities, and a fixed basket means the same real command over goods in every year, so the comparison is between periods in a stable unit. The consequence is that it is a measure of command over goods and not of relative position, so the same household can fall into poverty when its real income falls even though nothing about the distribution has changed, and a country can have a lower poverty rate with a more unequal distribution. That is the intended use and also the main criticism, since a line fixed in one country's basket is not obviously the right basket for another.

options.text: Whether income is distributed evenly, since a fixed fraction of the median divides a distribution in two
options.misconception: describes a share threshold rather than a measure of the shape of the distribution

options.text: Whether a household falls far behind the middle of its own society, and it cannot fall as the society gets richer
Whether a household is poor in a fixed sense, because the median is itself the fixed reference point

Two properties follow directly. A society in which every income doubles has the same relative poverty rate, because the median doubles with it, and it will have no absolute poverty if the poorest can now buy what they could not before. The measure is therefore useful for comparing inequality between societies and for tracking whether the bottom is keeping pace, and it is unsuitable for measuring whether anyone is going hungry.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Poverty in a recession
questions.learningObjective: explain why measured poverty can rise in an economy whose output is growing
questions.stem: Poverty can rise in a year in which real output is growing. What has to happen to the income distribution for that to happen, and why is it not a contradiction?

answer.exemplar: The poor can be made worse off while output rises if the gains are concentrated at the top of the distribution and if the poor lose in a second way as well, which is typical because the poor hold a larger share of their wealth in the form of assets whose prices fall in a slowdown, and because a rise in unemployment hits the bottom of the distribution first. Growth in the aggregate is a statement about a weighted average, and the bottom of the distribution is a small weight in it, so the average can rise while the incomes nearest the poverty line fall below it. There is a version of this that looks paradoxical, in which a distribution shift raises the mean and lowers the poverty rate at the same time, and it happens when the poorest are clustered well below the line: pulling the very poorest up does not move anyone across the line. Poverty and growth therefore measure different objects, and a growth rate is not a statement about anyone in particular.

questions.explanation: A rise in the mean income is compatible with a rise in the poverty count whenever the fall is concentrated in the households nearest the line and the rise in the households far above it, which is what a jobless recovery or a shift in the returns to different kinds of asset does to a distribution. The two series also differ in the units they are measured in, since the growth rate is a change in the level of output and the poverty count is a share of households, so a country can have rising output per head and more households below the line. What follows for policy is that a growth claim has to be accompanied by a distributional claim before it can be used to argue that poverty is being reduced.
questions.hint: Ask what a weighted average can do while one of the weights moves the other way.

A household's income is below a stated line in real terms, which is the condition the measure reports

options.misconception: describes vulnerability to a shock, which is a dynamic state rather than the mechanism itself

The third statement is the definition of the measure and says nothing about dynamics, since a household can be below the line for one year for reasons that have nothing to do with any mechanism. The fourth is close but distinct, because it describes a household that is currently counted as not poor and yet is one shock away from being counted as poor, which is a statement about vulnerability rather than about reproduction.
questions.hint: Ask which statements explain why a position persists, rather than report where a household sits.

A multidimensional index therefore adds dimensions and, in doing so, has to make the choice the monetary measure avoids: how much a deprivation in one dimension is worth relative to another, which is a normative weight the index states openly. That openness is the measure's strength, since a reader who disagrees with the weights can recompute the index with their own, and a monetary line has no such knob but it also cannot register a household that has money and lacks a sanitation connection.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The marginal propensity to consume of transfer recipients
questions.learningObjective: state why a transfer to the poorest has a larger effect on spending than a tax cut
questions.stem: Why does a rise in a transfer to the poorest households usually have a larger effect on aggregate spending than an equal tax cut for the richest?

answer.exemplar: A tax cut for the richest household adds to its income at the margin at which a small proportion is spent, because the additional income is saved or invested, so the effect on aggregate spending is a small fraction of the amount. A rise in a transfer for the poorest household is also an addition to income at the margin, but the fraction of an extra unit of income that the recipient household spends is high, because the constraint that binds is a budget constraint on current consumption rather than a preference to save. The reason is visible in the budget: a household at the bottom has little wealth to draw on and a large share of its income going on consumption, so a transfer frees resources for current spending, whereas the same amount to a saver funds an addition to assets. That is why the multiplier attached to a transfer is larger, and why the ranking of two fiscal measures of equal cost depends on who receives them.

questions.explanation: The two measures differ in whose marginal propensity to spend they activate, not in the size of the amount, and the difference in propensities is itself a consequence of the distribution of wealth rather than a fixed parameter. A transfer to a household with little wealth relaxes a binding constraint on consumption, while a tax cut to a household with wealth relaxes a constraint that was not binding. The prediction therefore depends on the distribution of income and wealth remaining as it is, which is a limit on using the ranking to argue that a regressive tax cut can be made to work by size alone.
questions.hint: Ask what constrains the spending of each household before the change.

questions.stem: A government can pay every household the same flat amount or can test eligibility and pay only some households. Which statements about the two designs are correct? Select all that apply.

questions.explanation: The three correct statements are the standard arguments for and against targeting. A flat payment is simple, cannot be gamed, and cannot miss anyone, but the fiscal cost per recipient at the bottom is the same as the cost per recipient at the top. A test lowers the cost per recipient at the bottom and introduces three costs the flat payment does not have: administration, the incentive effect of withdrawing the payment as earnings rise, and errors in both directions, since a household can be wrongly excluded in the year its income falls and wrongly included through a misreport. Whether targeting is worth it depends on how large those costs are relative to the fiscal saving, which is an empirical question rather than a matter of principle.

questions.learningObjective: state what determines a worker's reservation wage and what it does to participation
questions.stem: A worker will accept a job only if the wage offered is at least some minimum. What determines that minimum, and what happens to participation if it rises?

options.text: The value of not working, which is the income from any unpaid activity, so a rise in that value lowers participation
The wage the worker is legally entitled to, so a rise in it raises participation without any change in preferences
options.misconception: confuses a legal minimum with a private reservation wage, which is set by preferences and other income

options.text: The worker's productivity, so a more productive worker has a higher minimum and a lower participation rate
options.misconception: links the reservation wage to productivity, which is a supply-side argument about the wage not a minimum

options.text: The number of jobs available, so the minimum falls when there are more vacancies, holding preferences fixed
options.misconception: makes the reservation wage depend on the demand side, which it does not in the standard account

questions.explanation: Taking a job means giving up whatever the worker would otherwise have, so the minimum acceptable wage is the value of that alternative, which is why it rises with unearned income, with the value of unpaid work at home, and with any benefit that is withdrawn as earnings rise. Because participation requires the offered wage to clear that minimum, a rise in the minimum reduces the number of people who accept any given wage offer, which is the mechanism through which a benefit increase can reduce measured participation. The reservation wage is a property of the worker, which is why it can be pinned down by observed participation and wages only jointly rather than from either alone.
questions.hint: Ask what the worker gives up by accepting the job, and how that enters the decision.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Compensating wage differentials
questions.learningObjective: explain how unpleasant characteristics of a job are paid for
questions.stem: Some jobs pay more than others. What explains a wage premium for a job that is unpleasant or risky?

options.text: The premium reflects that such workers are more productive, since unpleasant jobs attract the more able people
options.misconception: confuses a selection effect with a compensating differential, which is not what a premium requires

options.text: The premium compensates workers for the cost of the characteristic, so it equals the amount they would pay to avoid it
The premium reflects a shortage of workers willing to do the job, which is a market price like any other
options.misconception: describes a supply shortage, which would raise the wage but not for the reason a differential does

options.text: The premium exists only where a union sets the wage, since an unconstrained market leaves no room for compensation
options.misconception: supposes compensating differentials arise from bargaining rather than from workers' preferences

questions.explanation: A worker who takes a risky job gives up something, and the premium has to be at least the value of that something or the worker will not take the job, so in equilibrium the premium equals the compensating amount. The prediction that follows is that a rise in the risk should raise the premium, and that the premium should be larger where the workers have better alternatives, which is why the same job can carry a different premium in different places. The test of the theory is therefore comparative: two otherwise identical jobs with different risk should differ in pay, and the difference should be where the differential says.
questions.hint: Ask what a worker must be paid to accept the job rather than the alternative.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The wage markdown in a monopsonist
questions.learningObjective: explain why an employer with wage-setting power pays below average productivity
questions.stem: An employer with several hundred workers, none of whom is willing to travel far for a job, faces a wage-setting problem rather than a wage-taking one. Why does that employer end up paying less than the average productivity of its labour?

answer.exemplar: The employer recognises that raising the wage does not attract labour in the same proportion, because the workers it would attract are already at jobs they prefer, and the workers it already employs would accept a lower wage. The marginal revenue product of labour is therefore greater than the wage the employer pays, and the gap is the markdown. Since it is the same employer that sets the wage and receives the value, the markdown is not competed away in the way a competitive margin is, and it is converted into a rent to the firm or shared with managers. The aggregate consequence is the part that matters for the distribution: a country in which employers have wage-setting power over most of its workers will show a lower labour share for a given level of output and technology, and part of what looks like a change in the labour share is a change in the structure of the labour market rather than in bargaining over a given surplus.

questions.explanation: A competitive employer takes the market wage and the marginal revenue product equals it, because an employer who pays less loses the worker to someone who pays more. An employer with a local labour market has no such outside option, so the wage it pays and the value of what the worker produces diverge, and the size of the divergence is set by how unresponsive labour supply is where the employer operates. This is why the markdown is a measure of market power in the labour market, and why a fall in the measured labour share can be evidence about employer power, about the elasticity of local labour supply, or about the composition of employment, and the aggregate data alone cannot say which.
questions.hint: Ask what stops the employer from raising the wage until it equals the value of what the worker produces.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: A wage floor in a competitive labour market
questions.learningObjective: state the effect of a binding wage floor on employment in a competitive labour market
questions.stem: A minimum wage is set above the market clearing wage in a competitive labour market. What follows for employment, and on what does the size of the effect depend?

options.text: Employment rises, because a higher wage attracts more labour into the market than before
options.misconception: ignores that a price above the clearing rate reduces the quantity of labour firms wish to buy

options.text: Employment falls by the excess of labour supply over labour demand at the floor, and the size depends on the elasticities of both
Employment is unchanged, because a wage floor cannot alter how much labour a firm wants at a given wage
options.misconception: treats a binding floor as non-binding, which is what the premise rules out

options.text: Employment falls by exactly the size of the wage increase, since each worker displaced costs the rise
options.misconception: makes the loss of employment proportional to the wage change, ignoring the elasticities of both curves

questions.explanation: A price above the clearing rate creates an excess supply, and the employment level is determined by the demand side, since a firm hires workers up to the point where the value of what they produce equals the wage. A floor above that point moves the quantity of labour demanded down along the demand curve, and the more elastic demand is, the more employment falls. The conclusion is a statement about a competitive market, and it is the reason the same floor has a different effect where employers have wage-setting power, since there the wage is not the price at which the firm clears the market.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the labour market determines employment once the wage is fixed above the clearing level.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: A wage floor where firms can set wages
questions.learningObjective: state the effect of a wage floor where employers have wage-setting power
questions.stem: A wage floor is set in a labour market where a few employers hire most of the workers locally. What difference does that make?

options.text: The floor has no effect, because employers set their own wages and are not bound by a market rate
options.misconception: assumes employers pay whatever they like, ignoring that a floor binds where it is set

options.text: Employment falls as much as it would in a competitive market, because the same wage is being paid
options.misconception: applies the competitive result to a market where the wage was not a market clearing price

options.text: The floor can raise wages with little or no loss of employment, because the wage was already set below productivity
The floor raises wages and raises employment, since a higher wage always brings more labour supply
options.misconception: confuses the labour supply response with the firm's hiring decision, which is what the floor changes

questions.explanation: Where one employer has wage-setting power it is already paying below the value of what its workers produce, so a floor below that value can move the wage up without reducing the number of workers it wants at the new wage. Employment rises or is unchanged depending on how far the floor sits relative to the firm's markdown, and it falls only when the floor is pushed above the level at which the marginal worker would be worth less than the wage. This is the standard reason the two effects of a wage floor are treated as depending on the structure of the labour market rather than on the rate alone, and it is also why an aggregate employment effect has to be interpreted with the composition of the labour market in mind.
questions.hint: Ask whether the existing wage was already a market clearing price.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Efficiency wages
questions.learningObjective: explain how a firm can profitably pay above the market wage
questions.stem: How can a firm that pays above the market wage be maximising profit rather than losing money?

answer.exemplar: The firm is buying something with the wage that is not the worker's output as measured in the current period. A worker who is paid what the market would pay has no reason to make any particular effort, because the difference between effort and shirking is worth nothing to her at that wage, so a firm that pays above it can buy an effort norm it can rely on and can also reduce the cost of monitoring, of recruiting and of the quits that follow a bad experience on the job. The firm's problem is then the usual one of not being able to write a contract that specifies effort, and the wage above the market is the incentive that substitutes for the missing contract. A firm that pays the market wage cannot credibly return to a higher wage later, since workers will treat the higher wage as their right, which is why the premium has to be paid in advance and why the theory predicts the wage to be sticky rather than flexible.

questions.explanation: Any explanation has to account for why a firm that could cut the wage and hire someone else does not. The answer is that the wage is being used to buy an unobservable behaviour, so a firm that cuts it loses whatever that behaviour was worth, and the size of the loss can exceed the saving. The test the theory has to pass is empirical rather than logical, because the story predicts that the premium is larger where the work is more difficult to monitor, and that the effects of a fall in the wage are larger where the alternative employers are further away. It also predicts a floor on how far wages can fall, which is what makes the account relevant to unemployment and to why wages do not clear labour markets in recessions.
questions.hint: Ask what the firm receives from the extra wage, and why it cannot get it more cheaply later.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Implicit contracts
questions.learningObjective: state how deferred pay and tenure support an implicit contract
questions.stem: Employers often pay a rising wage with tenure and pay less than the current market rate for a newcomer. What does that arrangement do?

options.text: It rewards the worker for staying and for the training the firm has provided, so the firm's return on a leaver is limited
It makes the firm unable to cut wages in a recession, because the contracts it has written forbid it
options.misconception: describes an explicit contractual restriction, whereas the point is about unwritten expectations

options.text: It guarantees the worker a higher lifetime wage than a flat one, so everyone's lifetime earnings rise
options.misconception: ignores that the deferred pay is compensation for a specific pattern of behaviour

options.text: It shifts the cost of training from the worker to the firm, which is a gain to every new recruit
options.misconception: concentrates the benefit on new recruits, when the deferred pay rewards those who stay

questions.explanation: Paying a new recruit less than the current market rate and then raising the wage with tenure is a way of holding a worker, because the value of the arrangement to the worker depends on staying to collect the higher pay. The firm faces the mirror image, since a worker who leaves has collected less than the firm's spending on that worker justifies, so the firm has an interest in retaining. Nothing is written down, so the arrangement depends on both sides believing that the firm will not cut the pay of those who have served, which is a prediction about behaviour under pressure rather than about a legal right, and it is the reason wages tend to be sticky in the face of a temporary fall in demand.
questions.hint: Ask what a worker gives up by leaving and what the firm has spent on that worker.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Relative wages and effort
questions.learningObjective: explain why workers care about their wage relative to colleagues
questions.stem: If workers care only about their own wage, cutting one worker's pay while leaving colleagues' alone should not change that worker's effort. Why do firms sometimes find the opposite?

answer.exemplar: A worker who discovers that a colleague is paid more for the same work has a reference point for what her own work is worth, and she revises the wage she regards as fair accordingly. If the firm's reason for the difference is visible, the worker concludes that her own wage is too low and reduces effort until the difference disappears; if the reason is hidden she may infer that the firm pays arbitrarily, which lowers effort for a different reason and over a longer run. The prediction is a knife-edge in the effort function, a steep drop in effort when a worker's wage falls below what a colleague earns and little response above that level, which is the feature that makes a wage cut for identifiable individuals riskier than an across-the-board cut that preserves every comparison.

questions.explanation: The reference point is the wage of comparable colleagues rather than the wage the worker could earn elsewhere, so the firm's choice of who to cut becomes part of the incentive problem. A worker who is paid less than a colleague for the same job has information about her own relative position, and responding to it by shirking is rational from her point of view even though nothing about the job has changed. The aggregate implication is that the wage structure carries information about fairness, which is a statement about the distribution of wages inside a firm rather than about the level of wages across firms.
questions.hint: Ask what the worker learns about the fairness of her own wage from a colleague's pay.

questions.topic: Insider and outsider interests
questions.learningObjective: explain how the interests of established and new workers diverge
questions.stem: Insiders are established workers and outsiders are recent recruits. Why can their interests in the level of wages diverge, and what does the divergence predict?

options.text: Both groups lose from any wage change, so their interests cannot diverge at all
options.misconception: denies the possibility of divergent interests between two groups in the same firm

options.text: Outsiders earn more than insiders at the same job, so the two groups differ in what they consider fair
options.misconception: asserts a pay gap between the two groups that the description does not contain

options.text: Insiders are unemployed and outsiders are employed, so the two groups face different labour markets entirely
options.misconception: reverses the definition, since insiders are the established employed workers

options.text: Insiders have training specific to the firm and cannot leave without losing it, so they resist a wage cut that outsiders would welcome as a way in

questions.explanation: A worker who has spent years acquiring skills that only this firm can use faces a much higher cost to leaving than a new recruit, so the two groups are differently exposed to the same wage decision. That is the standard argument for why a wage reduction negotiated with the established workforce can be blocked by exactly the people who have the least to gain from refusing and the most to lose, while a firm trying to hire in an expansion can find that an internal wage structure blocks the low wage it needs. The prediction is that wage rigidity is stronger where firm-specific human capital is high, and it applies to the level of pay rather than to the incidence of any particular tax.
questions.hint: Ask what each group loses by leaving, and who has more to lose from a wage cut.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Union coverage and the average wage
questions.learningObjective: explain why a rise in collective bargaining coverage can raise the average wage
questions.stem: Collective bargaining coverage is the share of workers covered by an agreement negotiated on their behalf. Which statements about the effect of coverage on average wages are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Coverage raises average pay directly for the covered workers, whose wages are set by agreement rather than individually
An employer facing a higher wage for covered jobs may substitute capital or non-covered labour, which lowers employment in those jobs
Coverage can raise the wages of workers who are not covered if they use the agreement as a reference point when negotiating
Coverage raises average pay only if it reduces the number of workers employed, so any employment loss is required
options.misconception: requires an employment loss for a wage gain, which is not part of the mechanism

questions.explanation: The three effects are the direct one, the substitution effect and the demonstration or reference effect, and they can operate at the same time, so the net effect of a rise in coverage on the average wage is theoretically ambiguous even though the direct effect is unambiguous. The substitution effect is the reason a coverage increase can be associated with lower employment in the covered sector, and the reference effect is why a unionised minority can raise wages in a non-unionised majority, which is one reason a single firm's coverage status is a poor guide to its pay and the industry average is used instead. The fourth statement is wrong because nothing in the mechanism requires employment to fall, and the two can move in opposite directions.
questions.hint: Ask what an employer and an uncovered worker do when a covered wage rises.

questions.topic: The incidence of a wage claim
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the wage a union claims from the wage that is actually paid
questions.stem: A union negotiates a 10 percent wage increase for a group of workers. Why is the 10 percent not what happens to their real pay?

options.text: A nominal agreement does not bind the employer, who can simply pay the old rate to new recruits
options.misconception: treats the agreement as unenforceable, which is what collective bargaining is for

options.text: A nominal agreement raises the real wage by 10 percent provided prices do not change at all
options.misconception: asserts a real gain of the full size, which ignores the price level entirely

options.text: A nominal agreement does not raise the real wage by the same amount, and part of the nominal gain is lost to a higher price level
A nominal agreement is always worth less than the same agreement indexed to prices, in every period and place
options.misconception: compares two instruments without reference to what happens to prices under either of them

questions.explanation: A negotiated figure is a nominal wage, and the real wage is that nominal figure over the price level, so a 10 percent nominal gain is a 10 percent real gain only if the price level is unchanged and slightly less if it rises at all. The size of the shortfall depends on inflation over the period of the agreement, which is why agreements are sometimes written with indexation clauses and why the coverage of such a clause is itself a subject of bargaining. What the agreement does determine is the nominal wage, which is the part the union can commit to and the part the employer has to cost.
questions.hint: Ask what the real wage is the nominal wage divided by.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The skill premium
questions.learningObjective: compute the skill premium before and after a demand shift
questions.stem: Skilled workers earn 20 and unskilled workers earn 12. A rise in the demand for skilled labour raises the skilled wage to 26 while the supply of skilled labour also rises and the unskilled wage is unchanged. What is the skill premium before and after?
questions.explanation: The premium is the ratio of the skilled wage to the unskilled wage less one, so before it is 20 over 12 minus 1, which is 0.6667, or 66.67 percent, and after it is 26 over 12 minus 1, which is 1.1667, or 116.67 percent. The second route is the difference in wages over the unskilled wage, 8 over 12 and 14 over 12, which are the same two numbers, and the ratio route is the one to prefer because the level of the unskilled wage has changed in many comparisons even where the premium has not. The increase in the premium is 50 percentage points, from 66.67 to 116.67, and it comes from the skilled wage rising with the demand for skilled labour while the unskilled wage is anchored by its own supply.
questions.hint: Express the gap between the two wages as a percentage of the unskilled wage, before and after.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why the skill premium can rise
questions.learningObjective: set out the competing explanations of a rising skill premium
questions.stem: The gap between skilled and unskilled wages has grown in many countries. What are the competing explanations, and why is the size of the increase hard to pin down?

answer.exemplar: The first family of explanations says the return to skill rose because of what employers now want: computerised production, the outsourcing of routine tasks, and the fact that a given level of measured output takes fewer routine inputs and more skilled ones. The second says the supply of skill did not keep up, so a constant demand for skill meets a smaller relative supply, and the third points at institutions, since a minimum wage or a collective agreement that compresses the bottom of the distribution mechanically raises the premium without any change in productivity. The measurement difficulty is that a proxy for skill is a proxy for education, and education itself has risen, so part of any measured rise is the reclassification of the same workers. That is why the empirical literature reports a wide range of estimates: they differ in which controls they include for the changing composition of the workforce, not in the arithmetic.

questions.explanation: Each explanation makes a different prediction about what else should move with the premium, which is what the evidence is used to discriminate between them. A rise in the relative demand for skill should show up in the tasks firms report wanting, a shortage of skill in rising enrolment, and institutional compression in a binding floor or a coverage change. Because the measured premium is a ratio of two wages and both are statistics derived from a survey with a changing definition of skill, the movement attributed to the premium mixes a real change with a change in the measurement, and any single estimate has to be read with the classification assumptions stated.
questions.hint: Ask what else should have changed under each explanation, and how skill is being measured.

questions.topic: Employment protection and the hiring rate
questions.learningObjective: explain how the cost of dismissing a worker affects hiring
questions.stem: Dismissal protection raises the cost of ending an employment contract. Why can that raise unemployment even when no worker is dismissed?

options.text: It makes a worker more expensive to hire, since the firm faces the dismissal cost if the worker does not work out
It raises the cost of dismissing, which directly increases the number of workers who lose their jobs
options.misconception: assumes a rise in the cost of dismissal must increase dismissals, when it reduces them

options.text: It lowers the wage, so the firm hires more, and the higher wage then explains the unemployment
options.misconception: describes a sequence in which the unemployment has a different source

options.text: It has no effect on hiring, since a contract begins before any of its conditions can apply
options.misconception: assumes future dismissal costs cannot enter a hiring decision, which is the whole mechanism

questions.explanation: The firm that hires a worker takes on an option it would rather not hold, because ending the contract later may be expensive, and the value of that option is part of the cost of the worker from the first day. So a rise in protection reduces hiring at any given wage, and the reduction shows up as a lower flow into employment rather than as a higher flow out of it, which is why a rise in protection can be accompanied by a higher stock of unemployment and no increase in dismissals. The effect is larger where the work is hard to screen, since that is where the cost of a bad match, and therefore the value of the option, is largest.
questions.hint: Ask what the firm is buying when it hires, and what a future dismissal would cost it.

questions.topic: Unemployment insurance and the natural rate
questions.learningObjective: state the channel through which benefit generosity raises the natural rate of unemployment
questions.stem: A rise in the replacement rate of unemployment insurance lengthens the average duration of unemployment spells. How does that reach the natural rate of unemployment?

options.text: A longer duration raises structural unemployment, because the skills of the long-term unemployed decay
options.misconception: confuses a channel that acts on the rate with one that acts on the composition of the unemployed

options.text: A longer duration lowers the measured labour force, so the rate falls as the denominator shrinks
options.misconception: assumes a longer spell removes the worker from the labour force, which would be reclassification

options.text: A longer duration raises frictional unemployment, so the same inflow is present for longer and the equilibrium rate is higher
A longer duration raises the cyclical component, because demand cannot find the workers it needs
options.misconception: misattributes to demand what the change in benefits has done to the supply of labour search

questions.explanation: The natural rate is the number of people unemployed at any moment divided by the labour force, and the number unemployed is the flow of entrants into unemployment multiplied by the average duration, so a longer duration raises the stock for a given flow. A more generous replacement rate raises the reservation wage of a searcher, which is the benefit foregone by accepting a job, and that is what lengthens the spell. The channel runs through the duration and not through the entry rate, which is why the natural rate responds to institutional generosity while the cyclical component does not, and why the effect is found in the duration data rather than in the flows.
questions.hint: Ask what determines the number of people unemployed at any moment, given the number entering each week.

What is the new natural rate?

options.text: 5 percent, since a longer duration lowers the number entering unemployment by the same proportion
options.misconception: assumes the inflow falls to offset the longer spell, when the inflow is stated to be unchanged

options.text: 6 percent, since two months of duration is one sixth of a year and the rate scales with the fraction of a year
options.misconception: converts months of duration into months of unemployment, which is not what the one point a month refers to

options.text: 3 percent, since a longer duration means fewer people are unemployed at any one moment
options.misconception: reverses the direction, treating a longer spell as a smaller stock of unemployed people

options.text: 7 percent, since a two month longer average duration adds two percentage points to the 5 percent rate

questions.explanation: The rule in the question is that each additional month of average duration adds one percentage point to the rate, so two months add two points, and 5 plus 2 is 7. The second route is the stock and flow identity, under which the number unemployed is the monthly inflow multiplied by the average duration in months, and the unemployment rate is that number over the labour force, so holding the inflow and the labour force fixed the rate is proportional to the duration. The direction is the part that a sign error would destroy, and the check is that a benefit cut makes workers search longer, which is a rise in frictional unemployment and therefore a higher, not a lower, rate.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The added worker effect
questions.learningObjective: explain why measured unemployment can fall when household income falls
questions.stem: In some recessions measured unemployment falls even though household incomes are falling sharply. What produces that movement, and why does it mislead?

answer.exemplar: The unemployment rate counts individuals without a job who are looking for one, and when the main earner of a household loses a job the other earners in that household move into the labour force to replace part of the lost income. Their entry raises both employment and the labour force, and the number of people counted as unemployed does not rise as much as it otherwise would, so the measured rate can fall while the loss of household income is severe. The effect runs through the definition of the rate, which is a count of individuals rather than a measure of resources, and it is strongest where a second earner is available to enter and weakest where the household has only one. It is the reason a fall in the rate cannot be read as an improvement in living standards without also looking at hours, earnings and participation.

questions.explanation: Unemployment is defined per person and income is defined per household, and the two come apart exactly when households have a second earner to call on. The additional entrant is counted as employed, so employment rises and the denominator of the rate rises with it, and the ratio can fall. Since the extra work is entered to replace lost income, the earnings of the household can be falling throughout, which is why any reading of a rate move has to be checked against earnings and hours worked rather than taken as a summary of household welfare.
questions.hint: Ask who moves into the labour force when the main earner of a household loses a job.

questions.topic: Statistical discrimination
questions.learningObjective: state how an employer can use a group average to infer individual productivity
questions.stem: Suppose every employer believes that the average productivity of one group is lower than another's, and each believes its own information is accurate. What follows?

options.text: Every employer pays the group more, since the average is a lower bound and the employers can observe the individual
options.misconception: assumes employers can see individual productivity directly, which removes the reason for the inference

options.text: The market rate converges to the average, so the group ends up with the wage that matches its true productivity
options.misconception: conflates the market wage with the average, which is what the employers wrongly believe

options.text: No employer can act on the belief, since the law forbids acting on a group average
options.misconception: asserts a legal prohibition that is not the mechanism in the model

options.text: Every employer pays that group less even though each knows its own assessment could be wrong, since no one has an incentive to test it

questions.explanation: If each employer's belief is based on a signal that is correct on average but noisy for the individual, and no employer can tell whether its own signal is unusually bad, then acting on the signal is individually rational and the wage below the true average is sustained. The reason the belief is not tested away is that the individual employee cannot reveal her own productivity to an employer who has no way of checking the claim, so a type of worker who is above the group average bears a cost she cannot undo. The result is a wage gap that persists without any employer disliking the group, which is what distinguishes this account from one based on preferences.
questions.hint: Ask whether an employer can find out whether its own signal about a given worker is wrong.

options.text: The two are identical whenever every household has the same number of earners, so no comparison is needed
options.misconception: correct as a conditional but useless, since the two are then the same object and the item asks why they differ

options.text: The number of earners in a household varies, so the same total is divided by a different denominator in each case
Income per person is always more unequal, because dividing a total by more members reduces the mean
options.misconception: assumes a more equal distribution follows mechanically from a larger denominator

questions.explanation: The two statistics divide the same household resources by different numbers, and because the number of earners per household varies with income, the two rankings differ rather than merely rescaling. Income per person is the right measure for what an individual has to spend, while income per household reflects the resources of the unit that pools and shares them, and the standard equivalence scales used to move between the two assume a particular pattern of earners within households. The choice therefore changes the measured inequality, and it is not settled by a matter of arithmetic but by which unit the question is about.
questions.hint: Ask what denominator each measure uses and whether that denominator is the same across households.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Under-reporting in income surveys
questions.learningObjective: compute the effect of replacing survey top incomes with tax record data
questions.stem: An income survey of 1,000 households reports total income of 40,000,000, of which the 100 richest households account for 8,000,000. Tax records for those same 100 households show 20,000,000. Substituting the tax record figure for the survey figure, what is the revised mean income per household?
questions.explanation: The revised total is 40,000,000 less 8,000,000 plus 20,000,000, which is 52,000,000, and over 1,000 households that is 52,000. The second route is the average plus the correction, since the original mean is 40,000 and the correction to the total is 12,000,000 over 1,000, which is 12,000, giving 52,000. The size of the revision, 30 percent on the mean, is the reason income distributions built only from surveys are known to understate the top, and the sign is the part that matters for a conclusion about inequality, since replacing a survey figure with a larger tax record figure can only widen the distribution it feeds.
questions.hint: Adjust the reported total by the difference and divide by the number of households.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Within-country and between-country inequality
questions.learningObjective: distinguish inequality between societies from inequality within one
questions.stem: The world income distribution can be measured across countries or within countries. Why do the two measures move differently?

options.text: A rise in the income of a poor country relative to a rich one reduces between-country inequality, while a rise of the poorest within a country reduces within-country inequality
The two measures are the same object computed twice, so they necessarily move together
options.misconception: denies that the two decompose different parts of the same distribution

options.text: Between-country inequality is always larger, since countries are more unequal than the households within them
options.misconception: asserts a ranking that is an empirical fact about the particular measure used

options.text: Within-country inequality has no effect on a cross-country comparison, since each country is a single observation
options.misconception: confuses the level of one observation with its effect on the dispersion of the set

questions.explanation: The same set of people can be sorted by country and sorted by position inside a country, and these two orderings are independent, so a change in one need not show up in the other. Convergence between a poor and a rich country reduces the dispersion across countries without altering anything inside either of them, and a redistribution inside the rich country leaves the position of the rich country unchanged in the cross-country ordering. Since policy acts on one of the two at a time, and the two respond to different instruments, reporting only one of them misstates where the inequality that matters is located.
questions.hint: Ask which comparison a change in a poor country's income relative to a rich one affects.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Redistribution and the growth of the pie
questions.learningObjective: set out the mechanisms by which redistribution can affect the growth rate
questions.stem: How can a more equal distribution affect the growth rate of output, and why is the direction of the effect contested?

answer.exemplar: There are two channels and they push in opposite directions. A more equal distribution raises the share of income going to households with a high propensity to spend, so a given fiscal cost buys more additional demand, which supports output and employment in the short run and can be worth a great deal when the economy is below full employment. The other channel is longer run and runs through incentives: a smaller gap between what the top and the bottom earn weakens the return to education and to effort for those near the bottom, and if that reduces the accumulation of skill the growth rate falls. The contest is not about whether both channels exist but about which dominates, and it is hard to settle because the two operate over different horizons and on different populations, and because a rise in inequality can be a symptom of a growth acceleration rather than its cause, so the direction of causation has to be established before the size of the effect can be quoted.

questions.explanation: A cross-country correlation between inequality and growth cannot answer the question, because a country that grows faster for unrelated reasons may become more unequal as it does, which is a reverse causal channel that the correlation cannot exclude. The evidence that does bear on the question is of a different kind, and the honest summary is that the short run demand channel is the one with the clearest mechanism and the longest run incentive channel is the one about which the estimates are least stable. That is why the distributional consequences of a policy have to be assessed alongside its effects on demand and on incentives rather than traded off against them as a single number.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the economy each channel acts on, and over what horizon.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The three questions a distribution statistic must answer
questions.learningObjective: order the questions that a distributional statistic has to answer
questions.stem: Order these five stages in turning a set of household incomes into a statement about the distribution, starting with the raw data and finishing with a distributional claim.

options.text: The unit of observation is decided, since a person and a household give different denominators
A sample of households is drawn, using weights so that the sample matches the population
The income concept is defined, such as market income, disposable income or a money measure at constant prices
Incomes are measured, and where the two sources disagree a decision is taken about which to use at the top
An index is computed and the result is read with the assumptions that produced it stated

questions.explanation: The order is forced by the fact that each step defines the denominator for the one after it, so nothing can be computed before the choices are made. The unit of observation has to come before the sample is weighted, because a weighted mean of person incomes and a weighted mean of household incomes are different objects. The income concept has to be settled before measurement, since a market income and a disposable income are different series and a nominal and a real measure are different again. The choice of source at the top matters because the two sources disagree precisely there, and the index has to be reported with the assumptions attached, since each of the four choices above can move it.
questions.hint: Ask which step fixes the denominator for the step that follows it.
